pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — What Ocean Animals Need (ages 5–7): ocean animals need food, shelter, and the right conditions (water, oxygen, suitable temperature) to survive — just like land animals — and different parts of the ocean provide for different animals' needs.
• Standards — UK (DfE): directly supports KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals; and Y1 basic needs of animals for survival.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS3-1 (relationships between the needs of organisms and the places they live); 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life in different habitats).
• Operational details: establish the shared list of needs — food, shelter/safety, and the right conditions — and that these are the SAME kinds of needs a familiar land animal has, met in ocean-specific ways (a clownfish shelters in an anemone; a crab hides in rocks; a fish feeds on smaller creatures; animals need the right water temperature and oxygen dissolved in water). Emphasise that DIFFERENT parts of the ocean suit different animals (warm shallow reef vs cold open sea), a first taste of habitat-matching.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~5–6): name what an ocean animal needs (food, a safe place, water it can live in). B (transitional, ~6–7): give an example of how one ocean animal gets food or shelter. C (early formal, ~7): compare an ocean animal's needs to a land animal's and say that different ocean places suit different animals.
bestPractices: Bridge from the familiar: start with what a pet or garden animal needs, then show an ocean animal needs the SAME things met in watery ways — making needs a universal idea.
Make each need concrete with a real animal (clownfish + anemone for shelter; a fish eating smaller creatures for food) rather than listing abstract nouns.
Introduce habitat-matching gently — a warm-reef animal wouldn't do well in the freezing deep — to seed the 'suited to its habitat' idea.
Include 'right conditions' physically: animals need oxygen (they breathe in water) and the right temperature, correcting the idea that only food matters.
keyRepresentations: A needs checklist (food / shelter / right conditions) shown for a land animal beside an ocean animal.
An animal-meets-need pairing: clownfish–anemone (shelter), fish–smaller prey (food), animal–right water (conditions).
A 'which ocean home suits me?' matching of animals to reef / open sea / seabed.
A shelter close-up showing an animal safe in its hiding place.
commonMisconceptions: 'Ocean animals only need water' — they also need food, shelter, and the right conditions, like all animals.
'Fish don't breathe / don't need oxygen' — they take oxygen from the water through gills.
'Any ocean animal can live anywhere in the ocean' — different parts suit different animals (warm reef vs cold deep).
'Ocean animals' needs are completely different from land animals'' — the needs are the same kinds, just met in the water.
'Shelter isn't important underwater' — many animals need hiding places from predators and rough water.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children discover that ocean animals need the same basic things as land animals — food, shelter/safety, and the right conditions (oxygen, which fish take from the water through gills while whales, dolphins and sea turtles come up to breathe air, and a suitable temperature) — met in watery ways, and that different parts of the ocean suit different animals. The row's preferred (proposed) approach lets children actively meet an animal's needs and watch a thriving cue respond, with a side-by-side comparison to a familiar land animal and a habitat-matching moment intended to make 'the right conditions' felt rather than recited. This reflects the row's design preference, not an evidenced ranking of media; the sources are unverified.

activities.title: Care for an ocean animal: meet its needs and watch it thrive
feedback: When each need is met, a thriving cue brightens so the child can see cause and effect: 'The clownfish is safe now that it's tucked in the anemone.'
If a warm-reef animal is placed in the very cold deep sea, it falters in the pretend scene: 'This home is too cold for this fish — where could it thrive instead?' then recovers when moved back.
On the comparison panel: 'A rabbit needs food, a safe burrow, and air to breathe — your ocean animal needs the same kinds of things, just found in the water.'
activities.rationale: Needs are intended to become concrete and causal when a child provides them and sees an animal respond, rather than reciting an abstract list. The habitat-matching moment is meant to make 'the right conditions' a felt need and to seed the habitat-suited idea. Bridging to a familiar land animal frames needs as a universal pattern. The thriving cue and drag-to-place are optional live-response mechanisms that make the learning concrete; they are not a required product feature, and their effectiveness is untested.
sourceClaims: Most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals.
There are relationships between the needs of different organisms and the places they live.
Ocean animals need food, shelter, and suitable conditions (including oxygen taken from water and appropriate temperature), and different ocean regions suit different animals.
learnerActions: Choose a sea creature (e.g. a clownfish or a crab) to look after.
Give it food, offer a hiding place (tuck the clownfish into an anemone, the crab under a rock), and set the water conditions.
Watch a simple thriving/happiness cue brighten as each need is met.
Try a pretend habitat-matching step in the scene: drop a warm-reef fish into the very cold deep sea, watch it flag, then move it back to its warm home and see it perk up.
Compare the ocean animal's needs with a familiar pet or garden animal using a side-by-side needs list (food / shelter / right conditions).
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean animals need the same kinds of things as all animals — food, shelter or other ways to stay safe, and the right conditions — but met in the water; and different parts of the ocean suit different animals because conditions differ.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reef scene: who is meeting which need?
feedback: On a correct tap: 'Yes — the clownfish hides in the anemone, that's its shelter from predators.'
If a child says an animal needs only water: 'It also needs food and a safe place — can you find where it eats or hides?'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene pairs each abstract need with a concrete animal example, supporting the example-driven content. It is a useful introduction or recap; because the child reveals rather than provides, it does not itself elicit the act of meeting needs, so it works best alongside the care activity.
sourceClaims: Ocean animals need food, shelter, and suitable conditions (including oxygen taken from water and appropriate temperature), and different ocean regions suit different animals.
learnerActions: Explore a reef/sea scene and tap each animal to reveal which need it is meeting (tap the clownfish → 'shelter in the anemone'; tap a feeding fish → 'food from smaller creatures').
Point to an animal that is getting food, one getting shelter, and one in water that suits it.
Say in your own words what each animal needs and how it gets it.
activities.intendedInsight: Each basic need is met by a real animal doing a real thing — shelter, food, and the right conditions are all visible in the scene.

activities.title: Which ocean home suits me? Animal-to-habitat matching
feedback: On a correct match: 'The clownfish belongs on the warm reef with its anemone — that's where it thrives.'
On a mismatch: 'The deep sea is very cold and dark — would a warm-reef fish be comfortable there? Where else could it go?'
activities.rationale: Matching animals to zones makes habitat-suitability explicit and checks whether a child treats the ocean as uniform. It can verify classification and reasoning; for this age the deeper understanding may be better supported by enacting the care activity, so use matching as a complement or check, not the sole activity.
sourceClaims: Most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals.
There are relationships between the needs of different organisms and the places they live.
learnerActions: Look at several ocean zones (warm shallow reef, open sea, seabed, cold dark deep sea) and a set of animals.
Match each animal to the ocean home where its needs are met.
Explain why a warm-reef animal would not do well in the very cold, dark deep sea.
activities.intendedInsight: Different parts of the ocean provide for different animals; an animal must be in a place where its needs (right temperature, shelter, food) are met.

activities.title: Does the sea just hand it over? Talk it through
feedback: If a child says ocean animals need nothing: 'What does a crab eat? Where does it hide from predators? The sea doesn't hand it over — the animal has to find these.'
If a child denies fish need oxygen: 'Fish take in oxygen from the water through their gills — they do need to breathe, just in a different way.'
When a child maps needs onto a rabbit: 'Yes — food, a safe place, and air to breathe: the same kinds of needs, met in the water.'
activities.rationale: A short spoken discussion can surface and challenge the 'sea provides everything' and 'fish don't breathe' misconceptions through questioning and comparison. At this age such talk supports, but does not by itself provide-and-observe, so it complements rather than replaces the enacted care activity.
sourceClaims: Ocean animals need food, shelter, and suitable conditions (including oxygen taken from water and appropriate temperature), and different ocean regions suit different animals.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt: 'A child says ocean animals don't need anything — the sea gives them everything. Do you agree?'
Name what an ocean animal actually needs to survive.
Pick one animal (e.g. a crab) and say where it gets its food and where it hides — naming one thing it must find for itself.
Compare: does a rabbit need the same kinds of things as a fish? Which does the fish get differently?
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean animals must find and meet their needs; the sea does not automatically provide everything, and their needs match a land animal's, just met in the water (including oxygen, which fish take in through gills).

constraints: Target age is 5–7; keep needs concrete with real animals (clownfish + anemone for shelter, a fish eating smaller creatures for food) rather than listing abstract nouns.
Address 'the right conditions' physically: animals need oxygen (fish breathe it from water through gills) and a suitable temperature — not only food.
Bridge from the familiar: start with what a pet or garden animal needs, then show the ocean animal needs the SAME kinds of things met in watery ways.

A tap-to-reveal scene and a matching task check recognition/classification but do not by themselves elicit the act of providing for an animal; use them alongside the enacted care activity. This is an observable affordance limit, not proof one medium teaches and another cannot.
The thriving cue, drag-to-place, and zone-matching are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete — they are not mandatory and not product-specific.

Common misconceptions to watch: 'ocean animals only need water'; 'fish don't need oxygen'; 'any animal can live anywhere in the ocean'; 'ocean animals' needs are completely different from land animals''; 'shelter isn't important underwater'.

This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All listed sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
No source establishes that one medium outperforms another; efficacy of the enactment, tap-to-reveal, matching, and talk activities remains untested and is stated as proposed.

The source row records errorPatterns referencing a reteach prerequisite (mt_oAg79ju344) for the 'ocean is uniform' misconception; the prerequisite content was not available for this rewrite, so the matching activity states the warm-reef vs cold-deep contrast directly without assuming that prerequisite.

The original 'possible' rating for 3D and 'poor' rating for conversation are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical facts; conversation was retained as a supporting talk activity and 3D was not asserted to be useless.

probeDeeper: 'You said it needs food. WHERE does an ocean animal get its food and its shelter — does the sea just hand it over?'
'A rabbit needs food, a burrow, and air. Does a fish need those same kinds of things? Which does it get differently?' (land-animal comparison)
'Could a warm-water clownfish live in the freezing deep sea? Why not?' (right-conditions counterexample)
'Name one thing a crab needs that it has to find for itself.'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — ocean animals need the SAME basic things as land animals: food to eat, a safe place/shelter, and the right conditions (oxygen in the water, the right temperature). The sea doesn't magically hand them everything; they have to find food and shelter, and different parts of the ocean suit different animals. So an ocean animal's needs are much LIKE a rabbit's — just met in the water.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the sea automatically provides everything, so ocean animals have no needs of their own
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pick one animal (a clownfish) and ask: what does it eat? where does it hide from predators? Make each need concrete — the sea doesn't hand it over, the animal must meet it.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ocean animals don't need anything — the sea gives them everything
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says ocean animals need nothing; can't name food/shelter/conditions

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ocean animals don't need oxygen/air because they live underwater ('only land animals need to breathe')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain fish take in oxygen from the water through gills — they DO need oxygen, just get it differently. All animals need oxygen; the ocean supplies it dissolved in water.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ocean animals don't need to breathe because they live in water
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: denies fish need oxygen; thinks breathing is a land-only need

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every part of the ocean is the same, so any animal could live anywhere in it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a warm shallow reef with the cold deep sea — different animals live in each because conditions differ. Needs must be MET by the right place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't say different areas suit different animals; misses 'the right conditions'

responseLevels.gap: Says ocean animals need nothing, or that only land animals have needs / need to breathe.
responseLevels.full: Lists food, shelter and the right conditions (including oxygen), explains the animal must find/meet these (the sea doesn't just provide them), AND maps the needs onto a land animal — seeing the shared pattern of what living things need.
responseLevels.partial: Names one or two needs (food, shelter) but treats them as separate facts — can't connect to a land animal's needs, or misses that the animal must MEET its needs and that different places suit different animals.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says: 'Ocean animals don't really need anything — the sea just gives them everything, so they're not like land animals that need food and a home.' Do you agree? Tell me what an ocean animal actually needs to survive, and whether that's like or unlike a land animal such as a rabbit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands needs lists food/shelter/conditions AND maps them onto a land animal. A child with the 'sea provides everything' idea says ocean animals need nothing, or can't say they need oxygen/food, treating water life as effortless. The second tier (compare to a rabbit) exposes whether they see the shared pattern of living-thing needs or think sea life is a special case.
